title: A New Creation, Reconciled through Christ
english: … us” (John 1:14), and He underwent death in the flesh for the life of all, and so we have known Him; but from now on we know Him so no longer. For even though He is in the flesh, since He came back to life on the third day and is with the Father in heaven, yet He is understood to be above the flesh. For having died once, He “dies no more; death no longer has dominion over Him. For the death He died, He died to sin once for all; but the life He lives, He lives to God” (Romans 6:9–10). If, then, the Author of our life (Acts 3:15) has come to be in this state, it is altogether necessary that we too, following in His footsteps (1 Peter 2:21), be understood to be not in the flesh but rather above the flesh. Very rightly, then, does the inspired Paul speak.
“So if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation,” he says; “the old things have passed away; behold, they have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

For the old is the saying, “Earth you are, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19), and also that word in the book of Moses, “For the mind of man is intently set on evil from his youth” (Genesis 8:21). Old as well, besides these, are the things in the law. All these, he says, have passed away; for we have been justified through faith in Christ, and the power of the curse has ceased. He who trampled the might of death came back to life for us, and we have come to know Him who is God by nature and in truth, as we fulfil the worship in spirit and in truth (John 4:23–24), while the Son mediates and gives the world the blessings from above and from the Father. Hence the inspired Paul says very wisely: “All things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:18). For truly, the mystery of the economy in the flesh, and the renewal made through Him, are not against the Father’s will.

Our guide into the mysteries adds to this that the Father Himself reconciled us to Himself through Christ: us Greeks, who had been made His enemies by straying into the worship of many gods, and Jews, by wishing to stay fastened to the shadows of the law and not accepting the message of true worship. For through Him we have obtained access (Ephesians 2:18), and “no one comes to the Father,” as He Himself says, “except through” Him (John 14:6). So “all things are from God, who reconciled us through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18).

Notice again, I ask you, that although it was Christ who gave them the ministry of reconciliation, for they were appointed to apostleship through Him, he said that God was the giver. So they proclaim Him God, equal in glory to the Father, knowing that the two have one lordship and authority. What sort, then, is this word concerning the ministry, or what is the manner of the reconciliation? He goes on to say: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19), that is, He who was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ was God. For through faith in Christ, as I said, we have made peace with God (Romans 5:1), that is, we have been reconciled. And a clear proof of this is the forgiveness of our offences, which the God and Father grants; and the Son in turn, as God, extends it with authority, saying to the paralytic, “Your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9:2; Luke 5:20). So “in Christ,” that is, in the person of Christ, God reconciles the world to Himself, “not counting” their trespasses against those who have sinned (2 Corinthians 5:19).

Since, he says, we have been appointed to the sacred service of the gospel’s decrees, and the word of reconciliation has been placed in us (2 Corinthians 5:19), for we are God’s ministers (2 Corinthians 6:4), we must make entreaties to those who have believed in this way, for their own sake; and, taking up as it were the very person of Christ, we say to those who wish to drift away: “We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20), by believing in Him, that is, clearly, in the One on whose behalf we are ambassadors. For Christ is the door (John 10:9), and He Himself is the way (John 14:6).

But since it was likely that some would disregard the gospel preaching, count as nothing the truly “acceptable time” of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), and after this thrust the faith aside, our guide into the mysteries devises something more for them, well able to shame them and to persuade them readily not to …
translator_notes: Opens inside the quotation of John 1:14, begun at the end of the previous section.
Genesis 8:21 is quoted in its Septuagint wording (“intently set on evil from his youth”).
“We must make entreaties to those who have believed in this way, for their own sake”: the Greek clause has no verb, and “we must make” supplies the plain sense.
“The very person of Christ” renders τὸ πρόσωπον Χριστοῦ, the face or person of Christ: the apostles speak in His stead.
The section ends mid-sentence; it continues in the next section (“… fall back into carelessness”).
The column numbers of the Migne printing (PG 74, 353–355) are left out of the text.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in 2 Cor u04 rem early

title: Made Sin for Us, and Christ’s Gentleness
english: … fall back into carelessness, but rather to take firm hold of the life that is in Christ. And he says of the God and Father: “Him who knew no sin He made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him” (2 Corinthians 5:21). It is as if he were saying: He caused the One who had never sinned at all to suffer the lot of those who greatly love sin, so that He might show us, who have received faith in Him, to be righteous. For He endured “the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2); for One died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14), He whose worth equals that of all.

So when He is said to have become sin, do not suppose that He committed sin; for the Word, being God, does not know how to do wrong. Know rather that He was given by the God and Father for our sins, just as, under the law of Moses, they called the victims slain for sin “sins.” At any rate it is written in the prophets about those appointed to serve as priests: “They will eat the sins of My people, and in their iniquities they will take their souls” (Hosea 4:8). For under the law the overseers and ministers of the divine altars ate the sacrifices offered for sins.

It is a great means, then, of shaming those who would be careless, to ponder wisely that He who did not know sin was condemned with sinners and hung beside them for our sake, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him (2 Corinthians 5:21). For we have been justified by the God and Father “not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to His great mercy” (Titus 3:5), through faith in Christ.
“I, Paul, myself entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ,” and so on (2 Corinthians 10:1).

Many of the wise men of Athens lived among the people of Corinth. They regarded the Savior’s cross as foolishness (1 Corinthians 1:23), and they called the blessed Paul himself, the herald of the word of inspired Scripture, a charlatan and a babbler (Acts 17:18), together with the other saints. Some others of the circumcision, in turn, were setting upon the believers, praising circumcision and the sacrifices of the law, and saying that the blessed Paul was out of his mind, as one who had impiously chosen to make war on the ancient decrees. Against such men the zealous among the Corinthians were stirred up, and quite naturally; they wanted to lay hands on them as enemies of the divine preaching.

But the thing was most unseemly, and as far as could be from the gentleness that befits saints; for, as it is written, “the Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be kind to all, correcting his opponents with meekness” (2 Timothy 2:24–25). So he gives them a charge, saying: I, Paul myself, the priest of the divine mysteries, the steward and apostle, the one renowned for zeal, who spur you yourselves on to say with me, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21), entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, “who when He was reviled did not revile in return, when He suffered did not threaten, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). So at the right moment he brings them to remember the life of Christ, and makes them most meek and gentle.

I, Paul myself, he says, who am lowly when present among you face to face, not haughty, nor sharpened for quarrels and fights; who am bold when absent, I ask even now that when present I may not have to be bold (2 Corinthians 10:1–2). For, as I am minded to think, you will by no means take bold action against certain people who think that we walk, as it were, according to the flesh, that is, live in a fleshly way, in strife and jealousy. For, he says, “where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not fleshly, and walking in a human way?” (1 Corinthians 3:3).

Those, then, who wish to follow the Savior’s gentleness ought to rise above the suspicion of those men and not walk in a fleshly way. For if some disobey, one must not beat them down with clubs and force them, but rather wait for their willing …
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence: ἀναπίπτειν εἰς ῥᾳθυμίας finishes the last clause of the previous section (…καὶ πρὸς τὸ ἀναπεῖσαι ῥᾳδίως μὴ | ἀναπίπτειν, “to persuade them readily not to fall back”). Marked with a leading ellipsis; no words supplied.
Ends mid-sentence at περιμένειν δὲ μᾶλλον τὴν ἑκούσιον; the next section opens with αὐτῶν πρὸς Θεὸν ἐπιστροφήν (“their turning to God”). The paragraph ends with an ellipsis.

Negation and agency kept exact: the Father is the subject of “made sin” (περὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρός); μὴ ὑπολάβῃς ὅτι πέπραχεν ἁμαρτίαν, “do not suppose that He committed sin”; οὐ γὰρ οἶδεν πλημμελεῖν, “does not know how to do wrong”; δέομαι … μὴ παρὼν θαῤῥῆσαι, “that when present I may not have to be bold”; οὐ ξύλοις … καταβιάζεσθαι χρή, “one must not … force them”.
Hosea 4:8 is quoted in its Septuagint form, which differs from the Hebrew-based English (“they feed on the sin of my people”).

ἁμαρτίας ὠνόμαζον: the sin-offering victims were called “sins” (Septuagint usage of ἁμαρτία for the sin offering, for example Leviticus 4:24–25); possible allusion, not cited inline. The priests' eating of the sin offering echoes Leviticus 6:26 (Septuagint 6:19); possible, not cited inline.

συγκεκρέμαται: “hung beside them”, the crucifixion between criminals (compare Luke 23:32–33; Isaiah 53:12); possible allusion, not cited inline. δέδοται … ὑπὲρ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ἡμῶν may echo Galatians 1:4; possible, not cited inline.

ὁ ταμίας: “steward” (compare 1 Corinthians 4:1, οἰκονόμους μυστηρίων θεοῦ); possible allusion, not cited inline. ἐξεστηκότα may echo 2 Corinthians 5:13 (εἴτε γὰρ ἐξέστημεν); possible, not cited inline.
κατεπεφύοντο: “were setting upon” (καταφύομαι, to fasten on, attack).
The Corinthian zealots' wish to use force is Cyril's reconstruction of the setting; it is rendered as he gives it, without softening.
The column numbers of the Migne printing (PG 74, 356–357) and the page number 15 are left out of the text.
Divine pronouns are capitalised for clarity, which also keeps the Father (“He made”) distinct from Christ (“Him who knew no sin”) and from Paul (“he says”).
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in 2 Cor u04 rem mid

title: Weapons Not of the Flesh; Christ Speaks in Paul
english: … turning to God. “For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful through God” (2 Corinthians 10:3–4).

Those who know how to win renown in battle, and who rise against their enemies in a fleshly way, would quite naturally have fleshly armour; for they have helmets and breastplates, weapons and swords, and all the things by which they could conquer. But our wrestling and our manner of warfare need spiritual weapons (Ephesians 6:12). Indeed, the inspired Paul says very well that the one who is counted a soldier in Christ must be adorned with such splendid armour. He puts on him righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet, “and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,” and besides these “the shield of faith,” by which all the flaming arrows of the evil one are quenched (Ephesians 6:14–17).

So the arrows of the saints are not fleshly but rather spiritual and powerful through God, useful for pulling down strongholds (2 Corinthians 10:4), I mean the doctrines of the Greeks and of the heretics, and for showing their arguments to be rotten, utterly unskilful, and senselessly put together. “Let us then pull down such things, and every high thing raised up against the knowledge of God; and we shall take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). That is to say: let us pull down every height of impious notions raised up against God, and glorify Him with fitting words, imagining nothing lowly about Him. For we shall benefit others too, bringing them onto the right and most unerring path of thought, so that we may punish all disobedience once our own obedience has first been fulfilled (2 Corinthians 10:6). For great in the kingdom of heaven will be not the one who has only taught, but whoever is willing to add to his word the boast that comes from good works (Matthew 5:19).
“Since you seek proof,” and so on (2 Corinthians 13:3). “For we too are weak in Him, but we shall live in Him by the power of God toward you” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

He threatens those in Corinth who had sinned before (2 Corinthians 12:21) that, if they would not do what was fitting and live in holiness, he would not spare them again (2 Corinthians 13:2). The word “again” recalls the indignation he had already shown. And he tries to persuade them further that, should he rebuke those who stumble, his word will surely take effect, arguing as it were from what has already passed and from what is expected to come. This is why he says: “If you seek proof of Christ speaking in me” (2 Corinthians 13:3). For it is likely, he says, that you are waiting to see, the second time as well, whether Christ really speaks in me and carries His rebukes through to the end. Do not think, he says, as some who are still unbelieving and insolent think, that He is weak; for He is powerful among you (2 Corinthians 13:3), clearly among those who have believed and have come under Him, to whom He grants the care they need, and whom He turns back when they go wrong. So He is powerful among you; for He acts as God and shows the words of the saints to be true. And you will find my word strong in every way and at every point; for it is not I myself who speak, but rather Christ who is in me (Matthew 10:20).

But since he mentions those who, out of utter folly, supposed that Christ was truly weak because He endured the cross and bore the perversity, or rather the impiety, of the Jews, he makes a useful defence. He brings the power of the mystery forward at the right moment, and explains the willing self-emptying of the Only-begotten (Philippians 2:7) and the incomparable pre-eminence of the glory that came after it. “Yes,” he says, “He was crucified out of weakness” (2 Corinthians 13:4), as at least those still far from believing suppose among themselves; He suffered as man, and willingly endured death in the flesh. But they needed to know this as well: that having despoiled Hades and trampled the might of death, He came back to life on the third day, using not human power but power divine and beyond words.
translator_notes: Opens mid-sentence, finishing “… to wait for their willing turning to God” from the previous section.
“That is to say” renders ἀντὶ τοῦ, Cyril's formula for introducing his own paraphrase of the verse.
“And so on” renders κ.τ.λ., by which Cyril cuts short the verse he is quoting.
The column numbers of the Migne printing (PG 74, 358–360) are left out of the text. Column 360 falls inside the word δυνάμει (“power”), which is read whole; the text there is sound.
baehrens: PG 74; Fragmenta in 2 Cor u04 rem close
